11581-from-out-the-vasty-deep:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes wrote this 1921 novel around Wyndfell Hall, the real house its dedication names. The epigraph quotes Hotspur on calling spirits from the vasty deep, and asks whether they will come when called.

Miss Farrow sits by a log fire while her maid Pegler, grim and spare, refuses to sleep next door that night. She says she would not be fit for work tomorrow if she did. Later scenes move to a carved confessional, where a girl sleeps and is woken roughly. The novel is a ghost story built on dread, house, and servant talk.
1625-the-frozen-deep:
Wilkie Collins's The Frozen Deep opens at a grand ball in an English seaport, given to celebrate an Arctic expedition's departure. From the ballroom the story moves to the ice, where two rivals for a woman's love, bound by a prophecy of murder, face cold, hunger, and a choice between revenge and rescue.

Collins wrote the tale for Dickens's stage, and its scenes shift from dance to desolation with theatrical force. The frozen north becomes a test of character. The story is a compact melodrama of love, fate, and endurance, best read for its atmosphere and its ending.
20098-evening-round-up-more-good-stuff-l:
Col. Wm. C. Hunter published Evening Round-Up in 1915, with the subtitle More Good Stuff Like PEP. Hunter wrote pep talks for salesmen and business men of his day. He warns that too much pleasure can dull a person's taste for joy. People then chase wild thrills just to feel anything at all.

Such excess leaves them jaded and gloomy, Hunter argues in plain terms. His cure is steady work, cheer, and self-command each day. The pieces are short, brisk, and meant to be read fast. Readers get a dose of 1910s business pep in its purest form.
20312-out-of-the-deep:
Out of the Deep is a devotional book for souls in deep trouble and doubt. It asks if God's love changes when we cannot feel it. Is the sun's warmth gone because a storm is cold with hail? Is God's light gone because the world is black with cloud?

Such questions speak to readers shut in perplexity for a few days. The book urges them to recall God's covenant and take heart. Its title echoes the psalm that cries out of the depths. Readers get Victorian comfort writing at its most tender and direct.
21887-blacksheep-blacksheep:
Archibald Bennett is the willing errand-runner of his sister's household in Meredith Nicholson's novel Blacksheep! Blacksheep!, published in 1920. Mrs. Howard Featherstone spends much time thinking up jobs for her brother Archie. Her busy husband declines them all, but Archie has endless time and patience, and enjoys the work. The title comes from a verse by Richard Burton about outcasts sick for the homely fold.

Leslie L. Benson's pictures include a fugitive stopping at the crack of a gun. Nicholson mixes family comedy with flight and pursuit as the tale runs on. The blacksheep theme hangs over it: who is truly outside the fold, and who put him there? It is a light, quick novel of American manners.
22199-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Number 453 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal opened the September numbers for 1852, dated September 4. The weekly's three-halfpenny miscellany here turns to volcanoes. Extinct volcanoes, the writer warns, are not quite such safe neighbours as many suppose. They stand thick-sown in Britain, France, and along the Rhine, and some may not be as dead as they look.

Geology was thrilling news to the journal's readers, and Chambers fed the appetite. Tales, essays, and useful facts complete the number in the house pattern. The brothers Chambers sold self-improvement without dullness for decades. The mix of earth science and story shows their method still working in the autumn of 1852.
22533-life-of-schamyl-and-narrative-of-t:
Life of Schamyl tells the story of the Circassian war of independence against Russia. Schamyl was the Imam who led mountain peoples against the tsar's armies. The table of contents alone shows the war's long, hard course.

Chapters contrast Circassian and Russian modes of warfare in turn. Schamyl becomes Imam and continues the war despite setbacks. He issues proclamations and holds headquarters at Akhulgo. The siege of Akhulgo and the expedition against Dargo follow. His domestic life gets a chapter amid the fighting. Prince Woronzoff's march on Dargo shows the Russian side's effort. Readers get a nineteenth-century account of a famous resistance. It preserves how the Caucasus war looked to its own generation.
22617-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 454 of volume 18 in its new series, is a single weekly number of the famous Scottish magazine for family reading. The catalog record names no editor and truncates the date. The Chambers brothers built their journal on cheap, improving entertainment: essays, tales, and useful knowledge for ordinary households.

The sample comes from an essay on money and character, picturing people for whom money is like an extra limb of the body. Only when some sudden disaster cuts off the supply do they feel their first true monetary sensation, like a shock of icy showers. Such moral essays sat beside fiction and fact in every number. The issue preserves the voice of Victorian popular education at its most earnest.
23226-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Number 455 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, in volume 18 of its new series, is a weekly magazine of essays and information. One article in this issue takes up railways in Germany. It praises the small German powers along the French border for building lines with unusual energy.

Those states built not only for their own use, it says, but also to link up with lines in other lands. The result would be great trunk routes running through their lands. The writer calls the goodwill behind such junctions worthy of praise. Readers get a window on the railway age, when linked lines promised a linked Europe.
23562-studies-in-central-american-pictur:
Edward S. Holden wrote these studies in Central American picture writing for the first annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology to the Smithsonian, for eighteen seventy nine to eighty. It was printed in eighteen eighty one under director J. W. Powell. A table of contents and index, drawn from the full report, aid this separate issue.

Holden examines glyphs, signs, and painted records of Central American peoples, asking how pictures carry speech, dates, and history without an alphabet as Europe knew it. Original spellings and marked printer's errors are kept, with lists at the end. Scholars of Maya and Aztec writing will find an early, careful attempt to read picture systems on their own terms, a foundation stone for later work on Mesoamerican scripts.
23655-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Conducted by William and Robert Chambers, this weekly journal issue is dated Saturday, September 25, 1852, and priced at a penny halfpenny. Like every number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, it mixes biography, science, travel, and tales for a general reading public that wanted useful knowledge in an affordable form.

The leading article tells the life of Mrs. Chisholm, born Caroline Jones, who married a Madras army captain and went to India. Shocked by the state of soldiers' children in barracks, she founded a School of Industry for girls at Madras, teaching sewing, cooking, and household management. The issue preserves a mid-Victorian portrait of a celebrated woman philanthropist at work.
25643-he-giveth-his-beloved-sleep:
Elizabeth Barrett Browning writes this poem on sleep, printed in Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1882 with designs by Miss L. B. Humphrey, engraved by Andrew. Its text comes from Psalm 127, verse 2: he giveth his beloved sleep.

The poem asks what gift or grace surpasses sleep among all thoughts of God borne inward unto souls afar. Hero's hearts, poet's harps, patriot voices, and monarch crowns are set beside it, then little faith, dust, and bitter memories. Sleep, the poem insists, outshines them all as God's gift to the beloved. Humphrey's designs and Andrew's engraving give the poem a visual setting.
25995-as-we-sweep-through-the-deep:
Dr. Gordon Stables tells a sea tale of the stirring times of old in As We Sweep Through the Deep, printed by Nelson in 1894. Chapters run from poor Jack and an interrupted proposal to a battle and a breeze, a bolt from the blue, a ghost gliding away, and the saucy Tonneraire. A phantom Frenchman, a battle by night, mutiny, Cadiz, Camperdown, and Nelson and the Nile follow, with Willie dying a hero's death.

Wounded French prisoners aboard the Tonneraire marvel at kind treatment under surgeon M'Hearty, a rough, weather beaten sailor tender as any woman in heart. Patients wring his red hands and pray heaven to bless him. Stables, a naval surgeon himself, writes of old sea wars with salt, humor, and a warm heart for brave foes.
27710-lives-of-the-engineers-the-locomot:
Samuel Smiles, author of Character and Self-Help, wrote this life of George and Robert Stephenson, the locomotive engineers, in a new and revised edition published by John Murray of London in 1879. Its epigraph, from Pope, bids harbours open and public ways extend.

Smiles notes that since the book's original form, some seventeen years earlier, railway construction had made extraordinary progress. Great Britain, first in the field, had spent nearly 300 millions sterling on 8,300 miles of railway, then about 288 millions more on 7,780 additional miles. France, Germany, Spain, Sweden, Belgium, Switzerland, and Holland added mileage too. The book tells how father and son built the locomotive age.
28063-the-next-logical-step:
Ben Bova wrote The Next Logical Step, a science-fiction story about a computer built to simulate actual wars, complete down to the tiniest details, with missiles, bombs, and gas. The story opens with a CIA man telling General LeRoy and physicist Ford that he does not see what the problem has to do with him.

Eight senior officers of the General Staff have resigned or landed in the violent ward after one session with the computer. The general promises the CIA man a firsthand look, though it will take, Ford says, only a lifetime. Bova's tale turns war-gaming into a dark joke about deterrence and knowledge.
30441-canned-fruit-preserves-and-jellies:
Maria Parloa writes Canned Fruit, Preserves, and Jellies, Farmers' Bulletin number 203, published in Washington in 1917 under the supervision of the Office of Experiment Stations. Parloa argues that common fruits, though low in food value, still offer real health benefits and deserve generous, wise use, fresh and cooked.

Fruits supply varied flavors, sugar, acids, and bulky material that aids intestinal movement, plus potash, soda salts, and other minerals. The bulletin gives household methods for canning and preserving, turning seasonal fruit into safe stores. It serves home cooks who want plain, tested guidance for jars, jellies, and preserves.
31570-a-taxonomic-study-of-the-middle-am:
William E. Duellman's A Taxonomic Study of the Middle American Snake, Pituophis deppei, was published as University of Kansas Publications, volume ten, number ten, pages 599 to 610, with one plate and one figure. It appeared on May 2, 1960. Duellman studies the pine snake Pituophis deppei of Middle America. His figures show Pituophis deppei deppei from Cumbres de Acultzingo, Veracruz, and Pituophis lineaticollis lineaticollis from Dos Aguas, Michoacán, at reduced natural size.

The paper sorts out the forms of this snake, their ranges, and their distinguishing marks, for use by other herpetologists. Taxonomic studies of this kind settle which names belong to which populations, and where one form gives way to another. Readers of reptile natural history will find a precise, specimen-based revision, grounded in museum material from Mexico and Central America.
31899-conservation-through-engineering-e:
Franklin K. Lane's Conservation Through Engineering, an extract from the annual report of the Secretary of the Interior and issued as House Document 572 in 1920, argues for constructive national policies on natural resources. Lane, Secretary of the Interior, writes amid a coal strike and a national stock-taking of coal as a national asset.

Its contents cover saving coal, saving coal by saving electricity, white coal and black, and the age of petroleum. They also cover oil shale, the Diesel engine, and a program of progress including garden homes, reclamation, and soldier settlement. Readers get a government report that reads like a manifesto: use engineering, not waste, to make America's resources last.
32750-the-sphere-of-sleep:
Chester S. Geier tells of Brad Nellon and Big Tim Austin crossing Titan in a gale of snow and ice. Nellon nurses a dark wish: kill Tim, and win Laura for himself. Tim, big, carefree, and kind, walks on unknowing beside him toward Tower Point, short of food and sure the whole venture has gone wrong.

A slip hurls Nellon into an unknown world behind a metal door and corridor, where lights and sliding doors obey a hidden plan. When he returns, the ship is gone and the valley lies empty. The tale turns on guilt, rivalry, and a sleep-like sphere where a murderer's wish meets its price.
33645-the-man-who-couldn-t-sleep:
Arthur Stringer builds a detective romance around a writer who cannot write. The narrator, a Canadian by birth and thirty-three years old, has lived nine years in New York and is regarded by friends as a successful author of Alaska stories. Now, he confesses, he is a failure, because a man who can no longer write can no longer be reckoned an author. Sleeplessness and a stalled career push him into other people's troubles.

Eleven chapters follow an ox-blood vase, a stolen wheel-code, a man from Medicine Hat, an irreproachable butler, Panama gold chests, a dummy-chucker, a Rialto rainstorm, and a thumb-tap clue. Stringer mixes first-person confession with brisk mystery plotting, and the book charms readers who enjoy an amateur detective drawn into crime by his own restless nights.
9807-scarhaven-keep:
J. S. Fletcher wrote Scarhaven Keep in 1922, a mystery of a coastal keep, a theatre, and a missing squire. Jerramy, thirty years stage-door keeper at Norcaster's Theatre Royal, opens the tale on a Monday morning of old acquaintances. Chapters follow Grey Rook and grey sea, the Greyle history, and a leading lady left on guard. A cablegram from New York, a torpedo-boat destroyer, and a steam yacht deepen the plot.

Later chapters bring a lie on a tombstone, footprints, and a squire's fate, till the keep gives up its secret. Fletcher writes with brisk, seaside suspense. A reader gets a taut postwar mystery, where stage folk and sailors share one strange case.

doe-osti-3893679-automated-framework-for: Metal 3-D printing builds parts layer by laser-melted layer — and those parts slowly deform under heat and stress. Bhatt and Messner built an automated framework for predicting creep properties of L-PBF materials. The automation predicts part lifetimes without months of manual testing.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EhrlicherJoseph:
Five days after President Kennedy was killed, the FBI was already tracing Lee Harvey Oswald's boyhood. A memorandum dated November 27, 1963 records that Joseph Ehrlicher, commander of the Louisiana Civil Air Patrol, confirmed Oswald's enrollment. Oswald had joined as a CAP cadet at Moisant Field on July 27, 1955.

The detail mattered because investigators were rebuilding Oswald's whole life, year by year. A teenage cadet enrollment placed him in a uniformed youth program in New Orleans, a fixed point in that timeline. The memo preserves the confirmation as the Bureau received it, in the first week of the investigation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nato-75-:
In 1997 NATO and Russia signed a charter meant to soften the blow of NATO enlargement. Svetlana Savranskaya and Tom Blanton edited this briefing book, number 864, published in July 2024. Boris Yeltsin, Russia's president, privately called signing it a forced step.

Documents show the Partnership for Peace, which included Russia and Ukraine, was only a holding pattern while enlargement waited. Clinton ran parallel tracks of enlarging NATO and engaging Russia, and both depended on Yeltsin personally. The tracks often collided, yet often won cooperation. The record captures a bargain neither side fully believed in, made by two presidents who needed it to hold.
nasa-tm-19690024482-transferable-technol:
Transferable Technology, issued for fall 1969, is a NASA catalog of booklets reporting new finds suited to many uses. NASA's Office of Technology Utilization published Special Publications and Tech Briefs for readers outside the aerospace industry. The finds came from NASA research centers, contractors, and subcontractors across the space program.

The special booklets explain new concepts, designs, techniques, materials, and components in depth. Some survey whole fields, while others detail one significant development. Tech Briefs are terse notices of new solutions to old problems, or novel answers to unusual ones. All listed items came out before June 30, 1969. The catalog addresses engineers, scientists, managers, and workers, and notes that students and news writers found the series helpful too.
scarhaven-keep: J. S. Fletcher wrote Scarhaven Keep, dated 1922. The contents list thirty-one chapters, opening with Wanted at Rehearsal, Grey Rook and Grey Sea, and The Man Who Knew Something. Later titles include The Greyle History, The Leading Lady, Hobkin's Hole, The Invalid Curate, and Beneath the Brambles. The second half turns to The Cablegram from New York, The Old Playbill, and The Lie on the Tombstone. It runs on through The Steam Yacht, The Peel Tower, and The Footprints. The list closes with The Greengrocer's Cart and Ambassadress Extraordinary.
the-frozen-deep:
Wilkie Collins wrote The Frozen Deep as a tale of the Arctic, framed by a grand ball in an English sea-port town. Two ships, the Wanderer and the Sea-mew, sail the next day.

The town ball honors the sailing of a hunt for the Northwest Passage. Among the dancers stand Mrs. Crayford, wife of a lieutenant of the Wanderer, and her friend Clara Burnham, a pale orphan girl who will stay with her. Talk turns on Clara's grave air and weak health. Collins builds a tale of two men who love one woman, parted by ice, fate, and a dark secret from the past.
